description: We are Team NorthStar, a group of university and high school students from Myanmar who come from computer science, data, and design. We share a love of space science and a simple belief: open NASA data should help the people who need it most. That brought us together for this year’s NASA Space Apps Challenge. Our goal with Farm O’Clock is a practical, honest tool that helps smallholder farmers and extension workers choose when to sow and which crop rotation to try.
summary: Farm O'Clock is a mobile-first web app that helps farmers and extension workers choose safer sowing dates and compare crop rotations. By dropping a pin anywhere on Earth, the app reads NASA POWER daily climate data and SRTM elevation. It replays the last 20 seasons across 14 candidate sowing weeks to rate drought, flood, and heat risk, showing "about N in 10 seasons go well" (the calibrated share of low-risk past seasons).   The app compares three rotation strategies (Baseline, Water-Conserving, and Soil-Rebuilding) against the farmer's goals, featuring interactive Rain and Heat "what if" sliders. It concludes with a practical plan and a field-check checklist in English or Burmese.   Directly answering the challenge, Farm O'Clock helps users explore resilient crop rotations and compare strategies. It matters because smallholders—including in Myanmar—often plant without long-term climate records. Farm O'Clock translates open NASA data into an explainable starting point that honors, but never replaces, local farmer judgment.
details:
What It Does

Farm O'Clock walks a farmer through 7 short screens:

  • Find your field: Search a place name, tap the satellite map, or press "Use my location" (the phone's location service). Pins dropped on water are refused, and built-up areas get a warning (ESA WorldCover land-cover check).
  • What the data says about this field: Cards show soil moisture, rainfall, heat, and terrain slope from NASA POWER and SRTM, plus field greenness and usually-bare months from MODIS NDVI, and a soil card (texture, organic matter, pH) from ISRIC SoilGrids.
  • Your crop and goals: Pick one of 8 crops and up to 2 goals (Save Water, Rebuild Nitrogen, Prevent Erosion, Extra Income). Optional constraints can be ticked (they are saved with the plan but do not change the scores yet).
  • Past seasons: A year × week grid shows the last 20 seasons for 14 candidate sowing weeks, each rated low / some / high risk, with the reason (drought, heavy rain, heat).
  • Pick your sowing date: A slider over the upcoming sowing weeks, shown as real dates. Each week shows drought, flood, and heat risk and "about N in 10 seasons go well". For a week up to 30 days away, an outlook card shows this year's chance of a high-risk season from a trained risk model. For weeks further out, it uses a seasonal-forecast hint where available, or says it is too early to tell.
  • 3 possible futures: Three 3-year rotations (Baseline, Water-Conserving, Soil-Rebuilding) are ranked for the farmer's goals, with water need, soil health, soil loss, and income where data exists. Rain and Heat "what if" sliders change the field drawing, re-rank the cards, and re-run the 20 past seasons to show how the best sowing week would change.
  • Your plan: A short plan in plain words, a "dig 15 cm, is the soil damp?" check, a field checklist, and a Share my plan picture card (phone share sheet, or a PNG download).
  • Note: The app is available in English and Burmese (EN / မြန်မာ switch in the header).

How It Works (Key Technical Details)

  • Season replay engine (web/src/app/api/replay/route.ts): Pulls NASA POWER daily PRECTOTCORR and T2M_MAX from 1 Jan 1985 to about 5 days ago. The long record places 14 candidate sowing weeks around the local rainy period. For each of the last 20 seasons and each week, it replays the next 90 days: driest 30-day rain, wettest 7-day rain, and days at or above 35 °C. Each is ranked against this location's own history and combined into low / some / high risk.
  • Calibrated chance (web/src/lib/confidence.ts): This is the share of good seasons, weighting recent years more (5-year half-life). It is then corrected with a calibration curve learned in backtests, and shown as "about N in 10 seasons go well".
  • Risk outlook model (Python, backend/): A logistic regression per hazard (any high risk, drought, flood, heat), trained with scikit-learn on 1987–2025 seasons at 9 sites (backend/train_risk.py) and served as plain JSON coefficients by a FastAPI service (backend/app/main.py). Inputs include the last 30/60/90 days of rain, and 30-day topsoil and root-zone wetness (GWETTOP, GWETROOT) and temperature, mostly as anomalies.
  • Seasonal hint for weeks 30 days to 6 months out: Open-Meteo Seasonal API anomalies (backend/farm/seasonal.py). Its skill is not yet validated (repo tasks.md §4).
  • Rotations (backend/farm/rotation.py, web/src/lib/strategies.ts): The year-2 partner crop is picked per pin from the share of its own season that went well in the last 20 years, FAO-56 irrigation need, and an FAO ECOCROP temperature fit. Water need uses FAO-56 crop coefficients × Hargreaves ET₀ from NASA POWER temperature (backend/farm/water.py). Soil loss uses RUSLE (rain erosivity from POWER rain, soil erodibility from SoilGrids, slope from SRTM; web/src/lib/erosion.ts). Income uses FAOSTAT national yield × producer price (web/src/lib/economics.ts). The final ranking still combines these with a transparent rule-based scoring function. The code calls it "a placeholder for the eventual XGBoost model" (strategies.ts L5).
  • What-if sliders: Rain −50 % to +50 % and Heat −6 °C to +6 °C. The backend re-runs the 20-season replay with rain × (1 + change) and max temperature + change (/v1/scenario). The final plan on screen 7 is computed at the default (no-change) scenario.
  • Greenness: MODIS NDVI from MOD13Q1 v061 (Terra, 250 m, 16-day), read through Microsoft Planetary Computer (backend/farm/vegetation.py L31, L41; the file header mentions MYD13Q1 too, but the code keeps Terra items only): cover now vs usual, and months that are usually bare.
  • Farmer reports: The "is the soil damp?" answer is saved as an anonymous observation (Supabase). Nearby reports (10 km, last 30 days) are blended into the soil-moisture card (web/src/app/api/environment/route.ts L14–33).
  • Plan text: A fixed English/Burmese template (web/src/lib/brief.ts). No AI or LLM service is called in the app.
  • Testing: Backtests in backend/eval/ and reports/README.md, including a 73-site test where the recommended week gave 36 % low-risk seasons vs 28 % for a random week, a spatial hold-out, and a FAOSTAT yield check (Spearman −0.30 between season stress and national yield, 133 site-years). The report also states the limits: the drought model does not beat the 20-year average on unseen regions, and the Dry/Normal/Wet verdict describes the past 90 days, not the future.

Benefits

  • Gives a field-specific starting point for the sowing date and rotation, from free, global NASA data plus open ESA, ISRIC, and FAO data, with no need for GIS skills.
  • Designed with a simple, intuitive UI/UX so farmers can use it effortlessly with no prior technical knowledge required.
  • Shows risk in plain words and colors, with the reasons, so a farmer can see why a week or plan is suggested.
  • Puts water use, soil loss, and income side by side for three rotations, which the challenge asks for.
  • Works on a phone, in English or Burmese. The plan can be shared as a picture.
  • Asks the farmer to check the ground (soil damp? seed available? local forecast?) before acting.

What We Hope to Achieve

  • A tool that farmers and extension workers in Myanmar and other smallholder regions can use to explore safer sowing weeks and soil-friendly rotations.
  • Better accuracy over time by adding more NASA data (SMAP soil moisture, GPM IMERG rain), local yield data, and validated farmer field reports.
  • Supporting, not replacing, local knowledge.

Tools, Languages, and Software

  • Languages: TypeScript (web), Python (model API and evaluation), SQL (Supabase schema).
  • Web: Next.js 16.4.6, React 19.3.0, Tailwind CSS 4.3.3, Leaflet 1.9 + react-leaflet 5, framer-motion, lucide-react icons, @supabase/supabase-js (web/package.json).
  • Backend: FastAPI, uvicorn, NumPy, pandas, requests (backend/requirements.txt); scikit-learn, XGBoost (compared in backtests only, not served), matplotlib, pytest (backend/requirements-dev.txt).
  • Hosting and services: Vercel (web and model API), Supabase (Postgres: cache, observations, saved plans), GitHub.
  • Hardware: None beyond laptops and phones.
